text: Last class: I think we could open with the numbers.
Today: the artist whose retrospective opens tonight paints in muted colors.
The artist who painted this worked in muted colors for thirty years.
The canvas which hangs alone is the most evocative in the show.
The artist whose retrospective opens tonight has never shown in Brazil.
The room where the small works hang is the quietest in the museum.
Up close, the brushwork is loose and the texture is layered.
The painting that everyone photographs is not the best one.

This is the tour I give when someone has twenty minutes. We start here, in the room with only four paintings on the wall, and people always ask why. The answer is that these works are quiet, and if I fill the wall you will walk past them. The restraint is deliberate. Eleven works in a room that could hold thirty. Now, the small canvas in the centre, Evening, Interior. Please stand closer than feels polite, because the texture is the argument. The surface is layered, and there are at least three earlier paintings underneath the one you can see. Nineteen ninety-eight is the year everything changes for her. She comes back to figurative work after a decade of pure color, and at the same moment the palette goes muted, grey and sand and one faded blue that appears only in the chair. And finally, the enormous one at the end of the corridor, the one everybody photographs. It is the boldest thing she ever painted, and it is not the best. The best is the small one you have just walked away from, and I hang the big one last so that you find that out for yourself.

People are not afraid of art. People are afraid of being caught saying something naive in front of somebody who knows more than they do, which is a completely different fear and a much easier one to solve. My formula has two parts, and I have never needed a third. Part one: name one thing you can actually see. The brushwork is loose. The palette is muted. The texture is thick at the window and flat in the corners. Nobody can argue with what is in front of both of you. Part two: say what it does to you. It makes the room feel like early evening. It reminds me of my grandmother's kitchen. That is your opinion, and it is unarguable too, because it is yours. What holds the two halves together is a relative clause. The canvas which hangs alone is the one I keep going back to. The artist whose palette went quiet after ninety-eight is the one I would collect. The evidence travels inside the sentence, so the judgement never arrives naked. And one last thing. The only sentence that really disqualifies you in a gallery is I do not know much about art. In thirty years nobody has ever asked me for my credentials in front of a painting.

First, you look for longer than feels comfortable, and you name one thing you can actually see: the brushwork, the texture, the palette. Then, you say what the work does to you, because that half of the opinion is yours and nobody can argue with it. After that, you attach the reason to the judgement with a relative clause, so the evidence travels inside the sentence instead of arriving later. Next, you place the work in the artist's story: what changed, and when, and whether this canvas comes before or after that change. Finally, you give your verdict in one sentence, and you say whether you would live with the work or only visit it.
